chunks.summary: An asynchronous (ripple) counter is a chain of flip-flops where only the first FF is clocked externally; each subsequent FF is clocked by the output of the previous one, so the count 'ripples' through the chain rather than changing all at once.
chunks.text: An asynchronous counter is one whose state does not change in exact synchronism with the clock. In the classic 4-bit ripple counter, the external clock is applied only to the CLK input of the first flip-flop, FF A. The J and K inputs of every flip-flop are tied HIGH, so each FF is wired to toggle on every negative-going transition (NGT) of its own clock input. The output of FF A drives the CLK input of FF B, the output of FF B drives the CLK input of FF C, and so on. Because each FF only toggles after the previous one has already toggled, the new count value 'ripples' through the flip-flops from the LSB toward the MSB rather than appearing everywhere at once. The four FF outputs D, C, B, A together form a 4-bit binary number with D as the MSB and A as the LSB. After the 15th clock NGT the counter has cycled through all 16 states (0000-1111) and the next NGT recycles it back to 0000, so this is a MOD-16 (full 2^4) counter. By convention, schematics are normally drawn left to right, but counters are typically drawn right to left so that the MSB appears on the left and the LSB on the right, matching how a binary number is normally written.

chunks.topic: MOD Number and Frequency Division in Ripple Counters
chunks.summary: The MOD number of a counter is the number of distinct states it cycles through before recycling; each added flip-flop doubles the MOD number and divides the clock frequency by 2 at that stage.
chunks.text: The MOD number of a counter equals the number of unique states it passes through before it recycles back to its starting state. Adding a flip-flop to a ripple counter chain increases the MOD number (an N-flip-flop ripple counter has MOD = 2^N states, i.e. counts from 0 to 2^N - 1 and then recycles). Because each flip-flop toggles once for every two toggles of the flip-flop feeding it, every stage in the chain divides its input frequency by 2 -- this is called frequency division. The output frequency of the very last FF in the counter is therefore the input clock frequency divided by the MOD number of the counter: f_out = f_clock / MOD. This is why ripple counters are also used purely as frequency dividers, independent of whether the count value itself is used.

chunks.summary: Because each FF in a ripple counter must wait for the previous FF to toggle, propagation delays accumulate along the chain, limiting the maximum usable clock frequency and potentially producing decoding glitches.
chunks.text: Ripple counters are attractive because they are simple, using the fewest components to implement a given MOD number -- no extra combinational gating is needed between stages. However, because each FF's clock input is driven by the previous FF's output, the propagation delay of each stage adds to the next, producing a cumulative propagation delay across the whole counter. If the clock period is not long enough compared to this total delay, the counter can produce transient, incorrect intermediate states before settling, which can be especially problematic at high frequencies or with a large number of bits. For proper operation the clock period must satisfy Tclock >= N x tpd, where N is the number of flip-flops and tpd is the propagation delay of a single FF. Equivalently, the maximum usable clock frequency is Fmax = 1 / (N x tpd). Because of this cumulative delay, asynchronous (ripple) counters are not well suited to very high frequency operation, especially as the bit count grows, and any digital logic that decodes the ripple counter's outputs may see momentary erroneous count patterns (glitches) while the ripple is still propagating.

chunks.summary: In a synchronous counter every flip-flop is clocked simultaneously (in parallel) by the same clock signal, and J-K logic is added so that only the flip-flops that are supposed to toggle on a given clock edge actually have J=K=1 at that time; this removes the cumulative ripple delay and allows much higher operating frequencies.
chunks.text: In a synchronous (parallel) counter, all flip-flops share the same clock line and are triggered simultaneously rather than one triggering the next. Instead of always tying J and K HIGH, each FF's J and K inputs are driven by combinational logic (typically AND gates) so that J = K = 1 for a given FF only when the outputs of all lower-order FFs are currently HIGH -- this is the condition under which that bit is 'due' to toggle on the next count. For example, in a binary up-counter the second FF's J,K = Q(first FF); the third FF's J,K = AND of Q(first) and Q(second); and so on. Because the propagation delay for any FF to respond only depends on that FF's own clock-to-output delay (not a chain of previous FFs), the total propagation delay of a synchronous counter is the same regardless of how many flip-flops it has, unlike a ripple counter. For a synchronous counter to count correctly, on any given clock NGT, only the FFs that are supposed to toggle on that edge must have J=K=1 at the moment the edge occurs -- all others must have J=K=0 (no change) at that instant.

chunks.topic: Counters with MOD Number Less Than 2^N (Truncated Counters)
chunks.summary: A basic N-flip-flop counter is naturally limited to MOD numbers that are exact powers of two (2^N); smaller MOD numbers are produced by forcing the counter to skip states, typically by asynchronously clearing all FFs the instant an unwanted intermediate count is reached.
chunks.text: A basic synchronous or asynchronous counter built from N flip-flops can only directly produce MOD numbers equal to 2^N. To build a counter with any other (smaller) MOD number, the counter is modified so that it skips part of its natural counting sequence. The standard technique: (1) find the smallest power of two, 2^N, that is greater than or equal to the desired MOD number, and build a basic counter with that many FFs; (2) determine which FF outputs are HIGH at the count value equal to the desired MOD number (the first state that should NOT occur); (3) connect those FF outputs into a NAND gate, and connect the NAND gate's output to the active-LOW asynchronous CLEAR inputs of all the flip-flops. As soon as the counter reaches the target count, the NAND output glitches LOW for an instant, asynchronously clearing every FF back to 0000, so that count value exists only as a very brief transient ('temporary state') and is never seen in normal operation -- the counter effectively skips straight from the state before it to 0000. Worked example: a MOD-6 counter is built by taking a basic MOD-8 (3-FF) counter and clearing it the instant it reaches count 6 (binary 110); the state transition diagram for this MOD-6 counter shows the states 000 through 101 in normal sequence, with a special 'temporary state' 110 that appears only for an instant before the NAND gate forces the counter back to 000. State 111 has no incoming arrow at all in the diagram, because normal counting can never reach it -- it can only occur if the FFs happen to power up in that state, and if that happens the counter recovers on the very next clock and self-corrects. Decade counters (any counter with 10 distinct states) and BCD counters (specifically a decade counter that counts 0000 to 1001) are common practical examples of MOD-10 counters built with this technique. The same NAND-clear technique generalizes to larger composite MOD numbers -- for instance, a MOD-60 counter (useful for seconds/minutes timekeeping, e.g. clocked at 60 Hz) can be built by cascading six flip-flops (Q0-Q5) with their CLR inputs tied together and driven by a NAND gate that decodes Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5 (representing the state that should not occur), so the composite counter cycles through 60 states before self-clearing.
chunks.figure_note: Page 16: state transition diagram for a MOD-6 counter -- 8 circles (states 000-111) arranged in a ring; solid arrows trace the normal sequence 000->001->010->011->100->101->000; state 110 (drawn dashed, labeled 'Temporary state') has an arrow INTO it from 101 but its outgoing arrow (dashed) goes back to 000, representing the brief transient before the NAND-driven clear fires; state 111 has NO incoming arrow (unreachable in normal counting) but is shown circled in red as a state that could only occur on power-up. Page 19: schematic of a MOD-60 counter -- six JK flip-flops labeled Q5..Q0 (drawn right to left), each with J tied to the output of an AND gate that ANDs together all lower-order Q outputs (ripple-carry-style AND chain, same structure as a basic synchronous up-counter), K tied HIGH via similar AND logic mirrored from J, CLK inputs all driven by a common 60 Hz input line, and all CLR (active-low) inputs tied together to the output of a NAND gate whose inputs are Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5 -- decoding the count where those four bits are all HIGH, which asynchronously clears the whole counter back to 0 after 60 counts.

chunks.summary: A synchronous down counter is built like an up counter but uses the inverted (complemented) FF outputs to feed the higher-order J,K control logic; an up/down counter adds a control input that selects whether the normal or inverted outputs feed that logic, so the same hardware can count in either direction and its state diagram has two conditional outgoing arrows per state.
chunks.text: A synchronous down counter is constructed the same way as a synchronous up counter, except that the AND-gate control logic feeding the higher-order J and K inputs is driven from the COMPLEMENTED (inverted, Q-bar) outputs of the lower-order flip-flops instead of the true outputs. This is because, when counting down, a higher bit needs to toggle when all lower bits are currently 0 (about to borrow), which is the moment when all the Q-bar outputs of the lower stages are HIGH. A more general and very useful circuit is the parallel up/down counter, which has a single control input, commonly labeled UP/DOWN, that steers the control logic: through added logic (typically a set of gates that choose between the true output and inverted output of each FF), the control input decides whether each higher-order stage's J,K inputs are derived from the normal Q outputs (count up) or the Q-bar outputs (count down) of the lower stages. Because the counting direction can change dynamically, the counter's state transition diagram shows two arrows leaving every state's circle instead of one -- a conditional transition -- where the actual next state taken depends on the logic level currently applied to the UP/DOWN control input at the clock edge (one arrow followed when UP/DOWN = 1, the other when UP/DOWN = 0).
chunks.figure_note: Page 20: schematic of a synchronous MOD-16 down counter -- 4 JK flip-flops (D,C,B,A) with control AND/inverter gates feeding J,K of each higher stage from the COMPLEMENTED outputs of the lower stages (labeled with bars, e.g. A-bar, B-bar, ABC-bar into the gates), plus an accompanying timing diagram showing Input clock and outputs A,B,C,D counting DOWN in binary (each bit toggling on the falling edge of the bit below it, mirrored from the up-counter waveform). Page 23: an 8-state ring-style state diagram (states 000-111, labeled CBA) where every state circle has TWO outgoing arrows, one labeled '1' (taken when Up/Down=1, going clockwise / counting up) and one labeled '0' (taken when Up/Down=0, going counter-clockwise / counting down) -- illustrating the conditional (Mealy-style) transition structure of an up/down counter.

chunks.summary: A presettable counter can be forced (loaded) to any desired starting value, either synchronously or asynchronously, using dedicated parallel data inputs; this is also called parallel loading the counter.
chunks.text: A presettable counter is a counter whose flip-flops can be directly set to any desired binary starting value rather than always starting from 0. This operation is called presetting or parallel loading. Loading can be either synchronous (the new value takes effect on the next active clock edge, after the counter's normal J,K/D logic is overridden) or asynchronous (the FFs are forced to the preset value immediately, independent of the clock, typically via their PRE/CLR inputs). A typical implementation uses each FF's asynchronous PRESET (PRE) and CLEAR (CLR) inputs: parallel data inputs P0, P1, P2, ... are each combined (through gates, often with the parallel-LOAD control signal PL) so that when PL is asserted, each FF is forced directly to preset (if its corresponding P_i = 1) or clear (if P_i = 0), loading the whole counter in one step regardless of the clock. Because the preset/clear act immediately rather than waiting for a clock edge, this scheme is called asynchronous parallel load. Presettable counters are useful whenever a counter must start counting from some value other than zero -- e.g., a down-counter that must start from a value entered on switches (as in a countdown timer).
chunks.figure_note: Page 24: schematic of a synchronous counter with asynchronous parallel load -- three JK FFs (Q2,Q1,Q0) each with PRE and CLR inputs; parallel data inputs P2,P1,P0 are each fed (together with an inverted PL / Parallel-Load signal) into a pair of gates per FF, one driving PRE and one driving CLR, so that asserting PL forces each FF directly to the value of its corresponding P_i input, independent of the clock; normal JK counting logic (an AND-gate chain building an up counter) still drives J,K for counting when PL is not asserted.

chunks.summary: Commercial 4-bit counter ICs (e.g. the 74ALS160-163 family) provide clock, clear, parallel-load, and enable pins plus a Ripple Carry Output (RCO) that makes it easy to cascade multiple chips into wider counters; the 74ALS190/191 family are similar recycling 4-bit up/down counters.
chunks.text: Standard IC counters package four flip-flops plus supporting control logic into a single chip. A representative example, such as the 74ALS160-163 family, contains four internal flip-flops triggered by a positive-going transition (PGT) at the CLK input, an active-LOW asynchronous CLEAR input, and an active-LOW LOAD input that lets the counter be preset to any value present on its four parallel data inputs (A, B, C, D). This IC family also provides an extra output pin, RCO (Ripple Carry Output), an active-HIGH signal that goes HIGH to decode (flag) the last/terminal state of the counter's sequence. RCO is specifically intended for cascading: connecting the RCO of one counter chip to the count-enable (ENT) input of the next chip in a multistage arrangement lets several counter ICs be chained together to build a counter with a much larger overall MOD number than a single chip provides -- e.g. two 74ALS163s cascaded this way to extend the counting range. The function table for this IC family (CLR, LOAD, ENP, ENT, CLK -> Function) specifies: CLR=L forces Asynchronous Clear (on 74ALS160/161) or Synchronous Clear (on 74ALS162/163, which clear only on the next clock edge); LOAD=L with CLK edge performs a Synchronous Load; ENP=ENT=H with CLK edge performs Count Up; and ENP=L or ENT=L (with CLK don't-care) forces No Change (count is held). Separately, the 74ALS190/191 series are recycling 4-bit up/down counters -- similar in spirit but organized as a single up/down count direction control rather than the ENP/ENT enable scheme.
chunks.figure_note: Page 27: TTL 74ALS160-74ALS163 function table, columns CLR, LOAD, ENP, ENT, CLK, Function, Part Numbers. Rows: CLR=L (X,X,X,X) -> Asynch. Clear (74ALS160 & 161); CLR=L (X,X,X, rising-edge CLK) -> Synchr. Clear (74ALS162 & 163); CLR=H, LOAD=L, rising CLK -> Synchr. Load (All); CLR=H, LOAD=H, ENP=H, ENT=H, rising CLK -> Count up (All); CLR=H, LOAD=H, ENP=L, ENT=X, CLK=X -> No change (All); CLR=H, LOAD=H, ENP=X, ENT=L, CLK=X -> No change (All).

chunks.summary: Decoding converts a counter's binary state into a recognizable output (e.g. one line HIGH per decimal value) using AND (active-HIGH) or NAND (active-LOW) gates that each detect one specific combination of FF outputs; BCD counters typically decode their 10 states to drive a 7-segment or individual-LED display.
chunks.text: As a counter's bit width grows, simply wiring each flip-flop output to its own LED becomes hard to read at a glance, since a person has to mentally convert the binary pattern of lit/unlit LEDs into a decimal count. Decoding solves this by converting the counter's binary state into a directly recognizable decimal indication. An active-HIGH decoder for an N-bit counter uses one AND gate per decimal value 0 through 2^N - 1; each AND gate takes as inputs the true or complemented output of each FF as required so that the gate's output goes HIGH only when the counter is in that exact state (e.g., for a MOD-8 counter, the gate decoding count 5 = 101 takes inputs C, B-bar, A). Each gate's output can then light an individual LED representing that decimal count. The same idea can be converted to active-LOW decoding by using NAND gates instead of AND gates: each decoder output is then normally HIGH and drops LOW only for the instant the corresponding count occurs. For a BCD counter (10 states, 0-9), the same decoding technique produces 10 output lines, one per decimal digit; rather than wiring these to 10 separate LEDs, BCD counters are usually decoded further (e.g. via a BCD-to-seven-segment decoder) to drive a single 7-segment display device showing the digit directly.
chunks.figure_note: Page 31: schematic of a 3-bit (MOD-8) synchronous up-counter (JK FFs C, B, A) with an active-HIGH decoding AND gate added at the top whose inputs are taken from the appropriate true/complemented FF outputs to decode one specific count value, driving an LED. The same style repeats with a NAND gate substituted for active-LOW decoding, and per BCD decoding for 0-9 (not separately re-rendered here, same visual pattern).

chunks.summary: A synchronous counter's behavior is analyzed by predicting each flip-flop's control inputs (J,K or D) for every state, using a PRESENT-state/NEXT-state table -- the sequential-circuit equivalent of a combinational truth table -- and checking whether the design is self-correcting (recovers from any invalid/unused state).
chunks.text: Synchronous counters are not restricted to plain binary up/down counting -- they can be custom-designed to produce any desired count sequence. To analyze (or verify) an existing synchronous counter design, the standard approach is to predict, for every possible state the FFs could be in, what logic level each FF's control inputs (J and K, or D) must have been in order to produce the observed next state; this is organized into a PRESENT state / NEXT state table, which plays the same role for sequential circuits that a truth table plays for combinational circuits. Applying this to a synchronous up-counter and drawing the resulting state transition diagram together with its timing waveform makes it possible to trace exactly how each bit changes on every clock edge. A counter design is called self-correcting if, starting from any of its normally-unused/invalid states (states that should never occur in the intended count sequence but which could occur on power-up), the counter's control logic still drives it back into the valid counting sequence within a bounded number of clock edges rather than getting stuck in an invalid loop; a state diagram will show this by having every invalid state's outgoing arrow eventually merge back into the main valid cycle. Counters can also be built from D-type flip-flops instead of J-K flip-flops. Because a D flip-flop has only one control input (D) instead of two (J,K), a D-type counter needs half as many synchronous control-input expressions to derive as an equivalent JK-type counter, but in exchange the combinational logic driving each D input is typically more complex than the corresponding J,K logic, since a single D input must fully specify next-state behavior on its own.
chunks.figure_note: Page 38: state transition diagram for a synchronous up-counter -- 8 states (labeled CBA: 000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111) with arrows forming the normal counting cycle 000->001->010->...->111->000; states 101, 110, 111 are circled/highlighted in red to indicate that even if the counter starts in one of these (normally unused, in a MOD-5 design) states, it is self-correcting and folds back into the valid sequence. Accompanying timing diagram shows CLK plus outputs C, B, A as square waves, with C toggling at half the rate of B, which toggles at half the rate of A, consistent with standard binary counting.

chunks.summary: A standard step-by-step method designs a synchronous J-K counter for any desired sequence: draw the full state transition diagram (including unused states), build a PRESENT/NEXT state table, derive the required J and K levels for every transition, then design and implement the combinational logic for each J,K input.
chunks.text: The common design method for a synchronous counter built from J-K flip-flops proceeds in these steps: (1) determine the desired number of bits (i.e., the number of flip-flops needed) and the exact desired counting sequence; (2) draw the state transition diagram showing ALL possible states of that many bits, including any states that are not part of the intended counting sequence (these must still be accounted for so the design can be checked for self-correction); (3) use the state transition diagram to build a table listing every PRESENT state and its corresponding NEXT state; (4) add a column to that table for each flip-flop's J and K inputs, and for every present-state/next-state pair, write down the specific J,K levels required to produce that particular 0->0, 0->1, 1->0, or 1->1 transition (this uses the standard JK excitation table: 0->0 needs J=0,K=X; 0->1 needs J=1,K=X; 1->0 needs J=X,K=1; 1->1 needs J=X,K=0); (5) treat each J and K column as its own output function of the present-state variables, simplify it (e.g. via K-map), and design/implement the combinational logic circuit that generates each required J and K signal from the present-state flip-flop outputs. A worked practical application of this whole procedure is driving a stepper motor: a stepper motor rotates in discrete steps rather than continuous rotation (a typical step size might be 15 degrees per step), and it can be driven in either direction (reversible) depending on the logic level of a direction-control input -- making the motor's step sequencer a natural synchronous-counter design problem, where the counter's states directly correspond to the motor's winding-energization patterns.

chunks.summary: PLD design tools such as Altera's Quartus Block Editor provide ready-made counter macro-functions (in the maxplus2 library) so a full-featured counter -- e.g. a MOD-16 up/down counter, or an application block like a digital clock's hours counter -- can be dropped into a schematic instead of being built from discrete FFs and gates.
chunks.text: Rather than always building a counter from individual flip-flops and gates, the Quartus Block Editor (and its underlying maxplus2 library) provides pre-built counter macro-functions that can be instantiated directly in a schematic to program a PLD. A full-featured MOD-16 up/down counter macro is one example: it exposes a clock input, up/down control, and other standard counter control signals, without the designer needing to derive the J,K or D logic manually. These library counters can also be used as building blocks in a larger application -- for example, a digital clock's hours counter (which needs to count 1 through 12, or 0 through 23, and wrap around) can be built by taking such a library counter macro, configuring it in the MegaWizard settings, and connecting it in a block diagram; the tool then produces simulation results to verify its behavior before it is used in a larger design.

chunks.summary: HDL descriptions of counters (e.g. in AHDL) declare the count value as a bit array register, then describe the state-transition behavior directly with an IF/CASE construct that increments the count each clock and resets it once a target value is reached, mirroring the PRESENT/NEXT state table used for manual JK design.
chunks.text: Describing a counter in an HDL primarily uses synchronous techniques: all flip-flops implied by the register are understood to update simultaneously in response to the same clock event, and all bits of the count value transition from their PRESENT state to their prescribed NEXT state at the same time. Conceptually, the PRESENT state/NEXT state table used in manual JK-counter design is the direct equivalent of the truth table used to describe the HDL's next-state logic. Writing a counter in AHDL (Altera HDL) starts by declaring the counter's output as a bit array (e.g. count[N..0]) rather than as N separate single-bit signals -- this is the first important step, since it lets the rest of the code manipulate the whole count value as one multi-bit number. The typical body of the code evaluates the current registered state (e.g. count[].q) and tests it against the desired highest count value; if the current count is less than that maximum, the description sets the NEXT-state value to count.q + 1 (i.e. count[].d = count[].q + 1), incrementing the counter by one on the next clock edge. When the counter has reached (or exceeds) the highest desired state, that IF-test becomes false, and the code instead assigns a NEXT-state value of zero, which recycles the counter back to its starting state -- directly implementing the truncated/MOD-limited counting behavior described in section 7-4, but in HDL rather than with a NAND-driven asynchronous clear.

chunks.topic: Wiring HDL Modules Together (Hierarchical Counter Design)
chunks.summary: Large digital systems are made manageable by hierarchical design -- subdividing the system into smaller modules and wiring them together at a higher level; a MOD-100 BCD counter is built by creating one MOD-10 BCD counter module and instantiating two of them, cascaded, in a top-level design.
chunks.text: Designing large digital systems is much easier when the system is broken into smaller, self-contained, interconnected modules -- this is the essence of hierarchical design. As a worked example, consider building a recycling MOD-100 BCD counter (with a synchronous clear) needed for, say, a two-digit decimal display. Rather than designing all 100 states of this counter as one flat block, the easiest approach is to first design a single, reusable MOD-10 BCD counter module (counting 0000 through 1001 and recycling), and then instantiate two copies of that module in a higher-level design file, cascading them synchronously so that the first module's carry-out/completion condition enables the second module to advance -- exactly analogous to how discrete BCD counter ICs are cascaded in hardware (see 7-7). The block diagram and simulation results for this MOD-100 BCD counter design show the two MOD-10 sub-counters wired together and their combined count sequence verified in simulation. A related design technique is decoding an AHDL-described MOD-5 counter: the AHDL SUBDESIGN declares a clock input and a 3-bit output q[2..0], creates an internal 3-bit DFF-based register count[2..0], connects all its clocks to the input clock, and then uses a CASE statement over the PRESENT value of count[] to explicitly assign the NEXT value (count[].d) for each state: state 0 -> next 1, state 1 -> next 2, state 2 -> next 3, state 3 -> next 4, state 4 -> next 0, and any other (unused/invalid) state also defaults to next 0 (making the design self-correcting), after which q[] is simply assigned from count[] to expose the register value as the design's outputs.
chunks.figure_note: Page 51: AHDL source-code listing for a MOD-5 counter subdesign named fig7_40 -- declares 'clock:INPUT' and 'q[2..0]:OUTPUT'; declares an internal 3-bit register 'count[2..0]:DFF' with the comment 'create a 3-bit register'; connects 'count[].clk = clock' (comment 'connect all clocks in parallel'); then a CASE count[] IS block listing Present->Next pairs: WHEN 0 => count[].d = 1; WHEN 1 => count[].d = 2; WHEN 2 => count[].d = 3; WHEN 3 => count[].d = 4; WHEN 4 => count[].d = 0; WHEN OTHERS => count[].d = 0; END CASE; finally 'q[] = count[];' assigns the register to the output pins.

chunks.summary: A state machine is a sequential circuit that steps through a set of predetermined states under the control of a clock and other inputs; the term 'counter' is reserved for state machines with a regular numeric count sequence, while 'state machine' is the general term used when the circuit's job is to control events rather than count them.
chunks.text: The term state machine refers to any circuit that sequences through a set of predetermined states, with its transitions controlled by a clock and possibly other input signals. The term counter is used specifically for sequential circuits whose sequence of states follows a regular numeric progression -- the things being counted are, at the hardware level, always clock pulses, but those pulses may represent many different kinds of real-world events (parts on a conveyor, elapsed seconds, etc.). The general distinction drawn between the two terms is one of purpose: a counter is commonly used to COUNT events, whereas a state machine is commonly used to CONTROL events (i.e., to sequence outputs and decisions based on both the current state and external inputs, not just to track how many clock pulses have occurred). Structurally, both counters and state machines share the same basic block diagram: a Memory block of flip-flops (clocked, holding the current state) feeds its outputs as 'controls' back into a Combinational circuit (gates) block, which produces feedback next-state signals returning to the flip-flops' inputs; the combinational block can also directly accept external Inputs. A separate Output circuit block produces the machine's outputs. In the Mealy model, external inputs are also allowed to feed directly into the Output circuit block, meaning outputs can change asynchronously (immediately, in response to input changes, not just on the clock edge). In the Moore model, that input path into the Output circuit is absent (outputs depend only on the current state), and the output circuit itself is optional -- so Moore-model outputs only ever change synchronously with the clock. A worked example of a Mealy/Moore-style state machine is a traffic light controller: it takes inputs such as a clock, a car-present sensor, and configurable green-light durations for the main and side roads, and produces a change flag plus the six lamp outputs (main road red/yellow/green and side road red/yellow/green), built internally from a delay sub-block (times the light phases), a control sub-block (sequences state), and a lite_ctrl sub-block (decodes state into the actual lamp signals) -- illustrating hierarchical HDL module wiring (7-13) applied to a genuine state-machine (not pure counter) design problem.
chunks.figure_note: Page 53: generic block diagram for counters/state machines -- an 'Inputs' arrow feeds a dashed-outline 'Sequential circuit' box containing 'Combinational circuit (gates)' on top (which also receives 'feedback' from below) and 'Memory (flip-flops)' below it (clocked by 'Clock', receiving 'controls' from the combinational block above); the combinational block's output feeds an 'Output circuit [Moore: optional]' box, which combines it with a second 'Inputs' arrow (annotated 'Mealy model has controls for outputs') that is explicitly crossed out and labeled 'Absent in Moore model'; the output circuit produces the final 'Outputs'. Side notes: 'Mealy model: output signals can have asynchronous changes' and 'Moore model: output signals are all synchronous'. Page 54: block-diagram schematic of a traffic-light-controller state machine with input pins clock, car, tmaingrn[4..0], tsidegrn[4..0], reset feeding into a 'delay' block and a 'control' block; 'control' outputs lite[1..0] which (along with delay's outputs) feeds a 'lite_ctrl' block that produces six lamp outputs mainred, mainyelo, maingrn, sidered, sideyelo, sidegrn, shown driving two 3-lamp traffic-light graphics (red/yellow/green stacked) plus a 'change' output flag from the delay block and an exposed lite[1..0] output.

chunks.topic: Register Data Transfer Modes and IC Registers (PIPO, SISO, PISO, SIPO)
chunks.summary: Registers are classified by how data enters and leaves them -- parallel or serial, in either direction -- giving four standard transfer modes (PIPO, SISO, PISO, SIPO), each implemented by a well-known family of IC shift/storage registers; serial data flow is called shifting, and feeding a register's serial output back to its own input is called rotating.
chunks.text: Registers can be classified according to (a) how data is entered into them for storage, and (b) how data is read back out of them. Parallel input of data into a register is described as a register load. Serial data flow through a register -- moving one bit at a time on each clock, toward one end of the register -- is called shifting, which can occur either to the left or to the right; if the serial output of a register is fed back around to its own serial input, that circulating movement is specifically called a data rotate. Combining input mode (parallel or serial) with output mode (parallel or serial) gives four classic register types, each with a standard TTL/CMOS IC example: (1) PIPO -- Parallel In / Parallel Out (e.g. 74ALS174/74HC174): a bank of D flip-flops that all load their new value simultaneously from D0..D3 on a shared CLOCK edge, with all stored bits (Q0..Q3) directly and continuously available at the outputs -- i.e., a group of flip-flops that stores multiple bits simultaneously with every bit of the value available at once. (2) SISO -- Serial In / Serial Out (e.g. 74ALS166/74HC166): a chain of D flip-flops where data enters one bit at a time at SER_IN, and on every clock pulse each bit moves one position toward the other end of the register, finally exiting one bit at a time at SER_OUT in the same order it was originally loaded in -- this device is a plain shift register with no direct access to interior bits. (3) PISO -- Parallel In / Serial Out (e.g. 74ALS165/74HC165, 8 bits wide): data can be loaded into all 8 internal FFs at once via parallel D0..Dn inputs (controlled by a shift/load control SH/LD), and then shifted out one bit at a time via SER_OUT on successive clock edges; because outputting is done by shifting, this and the SIPO/SISO devices below are always synchronous -- the clock must be present to move data one bit per active edge, in contrast to combinational logic which needs no clock at all. (4) SIPO -- Serial In / Parallel Out (e.g. 74ALS164/74HC164, 8 bits wide): data is shifted in one bit at a time at SER_IN, but every stored bit (Q0..Q7) is made continuously available in parallel at the outputs, letting a serial data stream be captured and then read out (or displayed) all at once.
chunks.figure_note: Page 56: 74ALS174/74HC174 PIPO -- four D flip-flops in parallel, each with its own D_i input and Q_i output directly available, all CLK inputs tied to a common CLOCK line (no interconnection between the FFs -- they load independently and simultaneously). Page 58: 74ALS166/74HC166 SISO -- four D flip-flops chained Q(n)->D(n+1) with SER_IN feeding the first D input and SER_OUT taken from the last Q output, all CLK tied to a common CLOCK line -- a plain shift-register chain. Page 61: 74ALS165/74HC165 PISO -- four D flip-flops chained in shift-register fashion (SER_IN into first stage, chained onward, SER_OUT from the last stage); each stage's D input is fed by an OR-of-two-AND-gates selecting between the parallel data input D_i (when SH/LD selects load) and the shifted-in bit from the previous stage / SER_IN (when SH/LD selects shift), all CLK tied to common CLOCK. Page 63: 74ALS164/74HC164 SIPO -- top diagram shows four D flip-flops chained as a shift register with SER_IN feeding the first stage and all of Q0..Q3 broken out in parallel; bottom diagram shows the full 8-bit part (74ALS164, labeled '8-bit shift register') with inputs A and B ANDed together into the first D flip-flop's D input, CP (clock, via inverter) and MR (master reset, via inverter) each buffered, and all 8 D flip-flops (each with CP and active-low CLR inputs) chained in series producing parallel outputs Q0 through Q7.

chunks.topic: Shift-Register Counters (Ring Counter and Johnson Counter)
chunks.summary: Shift-register counters feed the last flip-flop's output back to the first flip-flop's input: a ring counter circulates a single active bit around N flip-flops giving MOD N with no decoding needed, while a Johnson (twisted-ring) counter feeds back the INVERTED last output, giving MOD 2N from only N flip-flops but requiring one two-input decoding gate per count.
chunks.text: Shift-register counters are shift registers modified with feedback: the output of the last flip-flop in the register is connected back to the input of the first flip-flop in some way, so the register's contents circulate indefinitely instead of shifting new external data in forever. A ring counter is the simplest form: it is a circulating shift register in which the TRUE (non-inverted) output of the last FF feeds directly back to the input of the first FF. For a ring counter to operate correctly, it must start with exactly one FF in the 1 state and all the others in the 0 state; since flip-flops power up in unpredictable states, a small preset circuit (e.g. an RC network feeding a Schmitt-trigger inverter chain, such as two stages of a 74ALS14) is used to force the counter into a known starting pattern -- typically all-0s except a single 1 in one designated position -- immediately on power-up, before any clock pulses are applied to it. With N flip-flops, a ring counter has a MOD number equal to N (only N valid states -- the single 1 bit visiting each of the N positions in turn), and because at any instant exactly one distinct FF is HIGH, the counter's own outputs directly indicate the current count with NO extra decoding gates needed. In the Johnson counter (also called a twisted-ring counter), the INVERTED (Q-bar) output of the last FF is fed back to the input of the first FF instead of the true output. This 'twist' means that for a given target MOD number, a Johnson counter needs only HALF as many flip-flops as an equivalent ring counter would (MOD = 2N for N flip-flops, versus MOD = N for a ring counter), because the counter effectively counts through N zeros-then-ones fill-and-empty pattern rather than just circulating one bit. The trade-off is that a Johnson counter's states are not self-decoding the way a ring counter's are: it requires one two-input decoding gate per output count value (e.g., decoding count 0 from Q2-bar AND Q0-bar, count 1 from Q2 AND Q1-bar, etc.) -- but each such gate needs only two inputs, regardless of how many flip-flops the overall counter has. Very few ring or Johnson counters are sold as dedicated ICs; in practice it is simple to wire a generic shift-register IC (7-15/7-16) into either configuration. A few CMOS parts (e.g. 74HC4017, 74HC4022) are Johnson-counter ICs that include the complete decoding circuitry on-chip.
chunks.figure_note: Page 67: preset circuit for starting a ring counter in the 1000 state on power-up -- a resistor (1 k-ohm) from +Vcc to a node also tied to a 1000 pF capacitor to ground (an RC power-up delay network), feeding two cascaded inverting Schmitt-trigger buffers (labeled 74ALS14, stages 1 and 2), whose final output goes 'To PRE of Q3 and CLR of Q2, Q1, and Q0' -- i.e. on power-up this pulses PRESET on one FF and CLEAR on the rest, forcing the known starting pattern. Page 68: Johnson (twisted-ring) counter -- three D flip-flops in series (D->Q2, D->Q1, D->Q0), each stage's Q feeding the next stage's D, but the LAST stage's INVERTED output (Q0-bar) is fed back around to the FIRST stage's D input (the 'twist'); a table alongside lists the CLOCK-pulse-indexed sequence of (Q2,Q1,Q0), showing the values cycling through 000,100,110,111,011,001,000,... (6 distinct states for 3 FFs, i.e. MOD-6 = 2x3); a timing diagram below shows CLOCK plus Q2,Q1,Q0 each HIGH for 3 consecutive clock periods in an overlapping, staggered pattern characteristic of a Johnson counter. Page 69: for a 3-FF (MOD-6) Johnson counter, six 2-input AND gates (numbered 0-5) each decode one count value from a pair of true/complemented Q outputs (e.g. gate 0: Q2-bar AND Q0-bar -> output Q2'Q0'; gate 3: Q2 AND Q0 -> Q2Q0; etc.), alongside a table listing (Q2,Q1,Q0) -> Active gate number for all 6 valid states.

chunks.summary: Flip-flops, counters, and registers -- the major building blocks of sequential logic -- can fail from the same causes as combinational circuits (open circuits, shorts, internal IC faults), and are troubleshot with the same basic procedure: observe operation, reason analytically about possible causes, then use test equipment to isolate the exact fault.
chunks.text: Flip-flops, counters, and registers are the major components used to build sequential logic systems, and they are subject to the same general categories of hardware failure as any combinational logic system -- open circuits, short circuits, and internal IC faults among them. Because the underlying failure modes are the same, the basic troubleshooting procedure used for combinational systems still applies directly to sequential systems: first observe the system's actual operation (what it is doing versus what it should be doing); then use analytical reasoning about the circuit's structure to narrow down the set of components or connections that could plausibly cause the observed symptom; and finally use appropriate test equipment (e.g. a logic probe, oscilloscope, or logic analyzer) to isolate the exact fault. The main added wrinkle for sequential systems versus purely combinational ones is that a fault's symptom may only appear after several clock cycles (since state persists and accumulates), so tracing the clock and state signals over time is often essential.

chunks.summary: HDL register descriptions use bit arrays to represent register contents and use concatenation (combining specific bits in a chosen order) to describe parallel load, shift-left, shift-right, and hold operations, all as synchronous transfers happening simultaneously on one clock edge.
chunks.text: HDL techniques describe register storage using bit arrays, and describe how data moves into, out of, or within that storage using parallel or serial transfer statements. A key HDL construct for describing serial movement of data is concatenation -- grouping together, in a specific chosen sequence, some desired subset of data bits -- which is used to express operations like shifting: for instance, describing 'shift right' means concatenating the new incoming serial bit together with all but the last bit of the current register value, in that order, to form the next-state value of the whole register. A representative example uses four flip-flops that can perform four different transfer operations: parallel load (new external data replaces the whole register at once), shift right, shift left, and hold (retain current value, ignore the clock event for the purpose of changing data). Regardless of which of these four operations is selected, all the bits involved are transferred synchronously -- meaning they all move together, in a single clock edge, rather than one at a time.

chunks.summary: An HDL ring counter is a shift register that circulates one active bit through its flip-flops (modulus equal to FF count); because power-up states are unpredictable, the HDL is written so the counter always fills with zeros first, then shifts in a HIGH bit to start the intended ring sequence -- guaranteeing correct operation from any initial state without a separate hardware preset circuit.
chunks.text: A ring counter, described in HDL, is simply a shift register that circulates a single active logic level through all of its flip-flops; its modulus is equal to the number of flip-flops in the register (matching the hardware definition in 7-17). Because an N-bit register has 2^N total possible bit patterns but only N of them are valid ring-counter states (exactly one bit HIGH), there are always many unused/invalid states that could occur on power-up. Rather than relying on an external hardware preset circuit (as the discrete-logic version in 7-17 does), the HDL can be written so that, with a bit of planning, the counter is GUARANTEED to reach the desired valid sequence no matter what its initial (possibly invalid) state is: regardless of which state the counter happens to initialize into, the shifting logic is arranged so the register eventually fills entirely with zeros; at the moment it detects that all-zero condition, the logic shifts in a single HIGH bit to kick off the proper ring sequence from that point onward. In the AHDL code implementing this strategy, the serial input logic (using an equality comparison operator, ==, which evaluates whether the expressions on its two sides are equal) is written to test whether the current register value equals all-zeros, and if so, injects a 1 as the next serial input bit instead of continuing to shift in a 0 -- guaranteeing self-starting, self-correcting ring-counter behavior purely in HDL, with no separate analog power-up circuitry needed.

chunks.summary: A digital one-shot pulse generator can be implemented in HDL using the same internal-counting concept as a counter; a nonretriggerable one-shot ignores additional trigger pulses while its output is already active, while a retriggerable one-shot restarts its internal pulse timer every time a new trigger edge arrives before the current pulse finishes.
chunks.text: The concept of a counter can be reused to implement a digital one-shot (monostable) circuit in HDL -- internally, the one-shot's pulse duration is typically generated by counting clock pulses up to some target value, similar to how a counter's MOD limit is used to define a cycle length elsewhere in this chapter. Two behavioral variants are distinguished: a nonretriggerable one-shot ignores any new trigger input pulses that arrive while its output pulse is still active -- once triggered, it runs its full internal timer to completion regardless of further trigger activity, and only after the output returns inactive can a new trigger start another pulse. A retriggerable one-shot, by contrast, restarts its internal pulse timer every time a new trigger edge occurs, as long as that new edge arrives before the current pulse would otherwise have finished -- meaning a rapid enough sequence of trigger pulses can hold the output continuously active far longer than a single pulse's nominal duration, since each new trigger resets the countdown to its full starting value again.
